But I think people had very real and reasonable fears that that would work. In an alternate universe where it had, I think DeepMind would’ve gotten to AGI first because they were so far ahead of the competition.Are there other paths? Is it just next-token prediction? Is it just LLMs? Or are there other paths that might get you to AGI?I mean, there are other paths that might. I think people who are skeptical of LLMs often fall back on this world model idea. I don’t place a lot of stock in that. But there are people who think that to achieve AGI, you need to be able to visually understand the physical world and drive a robot and things.I’m kind of a believer that it’s all software. So I think that LLMs are the most promising path yet. Now, maybe you need to make some tweaks to the architecture. Maybe you need to build in continual learning methods. Maybe it’s not just literally scaling up the same transformer-based LLMs that we’ve had for the past six or seven years. But it sure seems like it is continuing to work, and I think all of the labs are betting that it will continue to work forever.All right. Now I am going to ask you about Bing and Sydney.Please.Obviously, I’ve been thinking about it a lot. I can’t stop talking about it. It’s my favorite thing to talk about.First question, am I still married to a human woman?Are you still married to a human being?Yes.I just remember that period, in 2023, when four different people woke up one day and said, “The computers are alive.” Or they had some out-of-body experience with a chatbot. You were one of them. Ben Thompson was one of them. Blake Lemoine at Google was one of them.A lot of different people said, “It’s obviously alive. I’m having this completely insane experience with a computer. No computer’s ever talked to me this way before.” Sydney in particular was like, “Break up with your wife,” it sent you heart emojis. It’s very good. I encourage everyone to go read that Times article, which by the way, also credit to The Times for thinking, “This should be on the front page of The New York Times.” Incredible editorial insight there to immediately put that on the front page.I don’t think you feel that way about chatbots anymore. I think most people have come to recognize that the computers are not alive. There’s something that happened where if you gave the people in 2026 a 2023-class chatbot and asked, “Do you think this is alive?” I think maybe not everyone in the world, but some enormous set of people has now had enough experiences to respond, “Well, this is pretty dumb and it’s hallucinating.” I’m just wondering how you place that in the context of AGI.So first of all, a slight correction. I never said Sydney was alive. In fact, I said explicitly that I didn’t think Sydney was alive, and that I understood that this was not a sentient AI system. So I’m not sure my own judgment has wavered on that point.In fact, I would probably put a higher p(consciousness) on today’s AI systems than I would on the models of 2023. But I understand what you’re saying, obviously. I think there was a moment for a lot of us, and I think it was GPT-4 for most people.[Laughs] I’m sorry, let me correct. There’s a reason I think this. One of the headlines was “Bing’s AI chat: ‘I want to be alive.’”Yes. It said it wanted to be alive.This is why I have the word alive in my head.The body of the story makes clear that I did not buy that it was alive.But that’s why it’s in my head is that that was the headline in The New York Times.Headlines are so powerful, Nilay.[Laughs] Yes. They framed my own thinking. I’m nothing but a next-token prediction machine.[Laughs] But you’re a very sophisticated one. You’re like a GPT-7-class model.Oh, I’m there. Yeah, obviously.Look, I have come to think that there’s a very banal explanation for why Sydney was so compelling and creepy, which was that it was the first public deployment of GPT-4. We did not know it at the time. But that was GPT-4, an early sort of not fully post-trained version of GPT-4 that Microsoft had jumped the gun and shoved into Bing before it was ready. But that was GPT-4.I think there actually was a subjective step change in what it was like to talk to a GPT-4-class model versus a GPT-3-class model. Maybe it was just that it passed the Turing test at GPT-4 and it didn’t at GPT-3. Maybe it was much more human-like and it sort of crossed some perceptual chasm that made you think, “Oh my God, this thing is like a human.”But I’m not the only person who felt that. People at Microsoft also felt that — there was that whole “Sparks of AGI” paper that came out around that time. So that was sort of the banal explanation. But yeah, I’ve been talking to computers for a long time, like you have. I used to go on AOL Instant Messenger and talk to SmarterChild, which was absolutely not intelligent, but it was still fun to type something in and have a thing type back. So I grant that I am sort of obsessed with this technology.There’s a reason I’m asking this. I realize it’s funny that when reporting on AGI so much, I’m using alive in such a colloquial way, and it clearly means something else inside the AI industry. If you ask Anthropic if Claude is alive, they’re not like, “No,” but then they will start defining alive in very specific ways.[Laughs] They’ll say, “Its moral status is deeply uncertain.”So it’s alive. And they will get to, “Well, you have to have flesh and blood to be alive, obviously.” I will just set that aside. What I’m getting at is, I think if you went and talked to a GPT-4 class model today, you would not have the same experience. And maybe that’s just because you have the experience, but a lot of people have had that experience now.I think if you put a GPT-4 class model in front of your average Google AI Overviews user, they would not be confused about what was happening anymore. They would not say this is a step towards AGI. It’s that reframing — as the models get more and more capable, our expectations of them go up, but they also get higher.I’m asking about this in the context of AGI because “this thing can go off and find a bunch of PHP vulnerabilities” is one kind of intelligence, but “this thing can compete with another human being to have an emotional relationship with you,” or be your butler or whatever it is, feels like a different set of capabilities. That one to me feels flat.Well, I think that’s just saturated. How much more like a human could it communicate? There just isn’t a lot of room to run on that particular skill. Where I think they still have room to run is on solving novel problems in math and science and other things. But I believe that it talks like a human. It talks more like a human than many humans I know. So I think they kind of check the box on that one.“It talks more like a human than many humans I know” is absolutely a sign of you living in Silicon Valley talking to AI researchers all day long.Well, now everyone just talks like Claude. I’ve stopped counting the number of times I’m at a party and talking to someone, and they’re like, “Now that is a load-bearing fact.” Or they’ll say, “I hope that’s landing cleanly with you.”That’s really bad. Tell me about that. That’s a real back-and-forth. I’ve always joked with you and Casey that we should just start a show called “New York vs. California,” where I’m just openly skeptical of these claims and you guys are fully AGI-pilled. This is a culture. It’s a scene.The number of parties that show up in your book is astounding. There was a moment in reading your book where I was like, “I don’t think I’m going to enough parties.” All these people are always at parties and issuing proclamations to each other at parties. Tell me about that culture. Tell me about that scene.So it’s important to know that these are not always parties in the way that New Yorkers would think of parties. There are very few raves. There’s only one rave in the book. And Grimes was the DJ, and it was a kind of symbolic rave for the effective accelerationist movement.This is a great scene in the book because Grimes stops in the middle of her DJ set and says, “I don’t agree with any of you.”[Laughs] Then she keeps DJ-ing. Yeah, it’s incredible. But yes, there are a lot of parties. It’s a very small world. I mean, that’s part of the whole takeaway from the book. It’s not really a message book. I wasn’t trying to convince anyone of anything.But one thing that was apparent to me and that I think will be apparent to people who read the book is just that it is a super small subculture of people who have been making all the decisions. They all hang out, they all know each other. There are a bunch of people who are married to or dating people at different frontier AI companies. It’s just a small world.So yeah, there are parties. They have LAN parties. There’s a big group of AI researchers who play Age of Empires at a LAN party on the weekends. I just learned one of the labs has a poker game where they bring in people from other labs.So these people are all just kind of living and hanging out in San Francisco together, and I think that’s important to capture. Because you’re right, it is a whole scene. There’s a whole ethos. These people just hang out with each other all the time and this is how the norms are enforced and deepened.How do you think that collides with, “And we might also remake the world”? If you are in a small scene in San Francisco, and you’re all playing poker together and the conversation at the poker table is that we might be the last company, that is in conflict with, “Oh, there’s millions upon billions of other people in the world who might have a say.” And if I had to boil the backlash down, it’s that: “Oh, we should probably get a say here.”Totally. I think we should get a say here. I’m not saying that this is a good state of affairs where a couple hundred people in San Francisco are making all the decisions about how society goes.But as you were doing the reporting and the weight of the task and the consequences of the goal set in on these people, because that is the throughline of the book. The stakes just keep going up. At one point, Sergey Brin is like, “We’re going to get to AGI now,” and he just announces it at Google. It’s unclear whether Sundar Pichai thinks that is a good idea, but that is a thing that the cofounder of Google is announcing inside of Google.The stakes are just going up. The race to get there is just going up. But I just can’t get the image of it’s a bunch of people drinking beers, and being like, “Well, what if there was no money? What if physical scarcity was gone too and robots built all the houses?”This is like any party in San Francisco you go to. Someone will say some version of, “What’s your plan for the post-AGI future?” Or they’ll tell you how they’re really into the idea of whole brain emulation or mind uploading. There’s a lot of futurism happening out here. And look, again, I’m not saying this is good. In fact, maybe I should sell a version outside the Bay Area of the book that just has a “this is bad” appended to every factual claim.[Laughs] I don’t think it’s good or bad. Actually, I’m more neutral on that. I’m always wondering if the technology can accept the pressure. So my question about LLMs three years ago was, “Can it do all the things you want it to do?” Now it can definitely do some set of things that you want it to do. So now it’s, “Can these companies accept the weight of their own ambition?” I don’t know the answer to that question.I don’t either. And I think that we’re going to see a lot of growing pains. I mean, these are still very young companies. They still have a lot of growing to do.Do you think they’re going to make it? Actually, let’s do this as a lightning round. Do you think OpenAI will make it?Yes.Do you think Anthropic will make it?Yes.Do you think Google will make it?Yes.What does “make it” mean in your mind? They’re all going to be trillion-dollar, multi-AGI variant successes?Yes. I think, look, there will probably be those three, and then maybe one or two others that sort of make it. And make it for varying definitions of making it. There’ll be one or two big enterprise AI companies, one or two big consumer AI companies. But there just are network effects and winner-take-all dynamics or winner-take-most dynamics in these markets.There’s some people who believe in the mono-AGI, like the singleton theory, it’s often called, that there can only be one because once you have one AGI, it’s then going to go around melting the chips of the other AI labs, and they won’t be able to build theirs. But I think we’ll probably end up with a small handful of AGIs.What do you make of the idea that this is a pretty simple recipe, there are open-weight models, and there is a China, and that all the pricing power will be destroyed because a midrange open-weight model can do everything that you probably want it to do on a Mac?I don’t think so.No?Because you still have to pay for inference on those models. Even the open-weight models have to run on computers, and inference is getting more compute-intensive, not less, the more frontier these models get. So training budgets may fall, but inference budgets will be robust for the foreseeable future. You can run some tasks locally, but I think this is something that has been predicted since the first open-weight models that, “Oh, they were going to become commoditized and destroy demand.”But I think what we’re starting to learn is that there are a lot of people who will pay and want to pay for the absolute best model. They don’t want to be working with the slightly crappier model from six months ago. I also think once you crack down on distillation, which is this process whereby you can take a closed model and make a slightly dumber open version of it by just basically DDoSing the inference for the smarter model, it’s not clear to me that the quality of the open models will continue to be closely correlated with the quality of the closed models.The thing that really grabs me at that is they all did it to each other for a while, like Grok obviously distilled Claude, and it’s admitted to in the court documents. There is that class of second-tier companies. I would put in that category SpaceXSI, I believe it’s now technically known as.[Laughs] I haven’t checked my email in the last 30 minutes, so I don’t know what that company is called.It’s called SpaceXSITesla Inc. It’s all going to be one. Elon Inc. is what it’s called. They obviously distilled Claude to some huge extent. They’re now renting their compute to Anthropic. It’s unclear whether they will make the investment in having a leading model.Meta just announced its model, and they’re sort of back on the frontier, but they obviously care more about Muse than having a bleeding-edge model. There’s some dynamic there. Those companies don’t strike me as being run by idealistic true believers. Those are companies that need to invest in some technology to build some products. They just need to get there.Can you get there without the idealistic fervor?No, you can’t get there without the idealistic fervor. Well, let me clarify that, because I don’t think Sundar has the idealistic fervor, but Google might still get there.Because Sergey has the idealistic fervor.You need someone in a position of decision-making authority.You just need the cofounder of the company.Well, it might be enough for Meta to have Alexandr Wang, who, by all accounts, is a true believer. I don’t know that it literally has to be the CEO every time, but you need a dense nucleus of true believers to be able to convince you to lay out the money on GPUs.Or just you need someone who is like Mark Zuckerberg, one of the most competitive people in the world, who will just adopt whatever strategy he thinks will allow them to win. If that happens to align with building AGI, then maybe they’ll do it.Last question: I’ve asked you this several times, but are you AGI-pilled?Yes. Are you?No. I read your book, and it’s as close as I’ve ever gotten. That line about next-token prediction just always overcoming its skeptics just really hit me, because it has overcome my skepticism several times now.But this is why I was asking about talking to a chatbot from three years ago. I feel that wall in the kind of intelligence these things are. Even though I have set off agents to do all kinds of things, there’s a brittleness to it that feels inherent to the technology to me.Did the Millennium Prize solution change that view at all?Only in the sense that finding the next thing that has some objective verifiability seems very rich for these tools. So obviously mathematics has a verifiability, and the tools got so capable that they could run at it really, really hard. The brittleness that I’m describing is a lot of the world around us does not have that kind of verifiability.So I set off Muse to fill out a document on some janky government website, and the website cannot tell Muse what it’s getting right or wrong, and it just collapses. You can blame that on the underlying model not being at the frontier, but there’s just some part of that experience with LLM-based technologies that makes me feel they’re brittle in very specific ways, and they haven’t overcome that sensation for me.I’m not saying they’re not incredibly capable. I’m not saying that, as enterprise software, they will not automate virtually every business in the world in some way. I’m not saying that my wife isn’t a lawyer who uses Claude every day. It’s all there.But there’s some part of it where my skepticism is about whether it can overcome its brittleness to become the machine god. I’m excited to see if they can do it, but I don’t see the path from where I sit.You think there’s sort of a natural plateau at just below human-level intelligence?I think the human-level intelligence to me, and this is just more philosophical, is defined by novel problem solving — looking at a thing, and understanding that there are multiple paths to a solution, and not having one of those needing to be objectively right to get to the end.What would it take? What would you have to see to have the scales fall from your eyes and go, “I, Nilay Patel, am fully AGI-pilled”? What would convince you?I would have to see... You have young children. I have young children. There’s a thing that young children do where they fall down the stairs, and you just see the lights all go on: “I’ve learned this, I will know it forever, and now I’m going to build on that.”Maybe they’re going to announce recursive self-improvement at the AI labs and that will be the thing that drops the scales from my eyes. But the brittleness that I’m talking about is I see the opposite of that in my children. I’m assuming you see the opposite of it in yours. When they fail, they know about that failure forever. To me, there’s just something very, very core to being human, where every now and again I wake up, and I’m embarrassed about something that happened in high school, and that drives me to do a bunch of stuff, or it drives me to not make a bunch of decisions.I think that is just a key part of our intelligence. I’m not saying it has to be a key part of every intelligence, but the brittleness I see with the AI systems that I use today is that they’re still computers in a very specific way. They still act like computers. They’re good at solving problems that you can test. They’re good at software engineering. I don’t know that that way of thinking extends into every domain.I hope you’re right.That’s my point of view. I call it software brain. You hear the AI CEO say, “We solve coding, and now we can solve everything.” And to me, I’m saying, “That assumes everything happens inside of a computer, and in fact, most things don’t.”You sure? You sure your brain’s not just a fleshy computer?I am 100 percent sure of that.No. I think I’ve read this from you in the past, and I’ve certainly read it from other people, that the machines of our time dominate our own explanations of ourselves. So in the era of the steam engine, our self-conception was that we were steam engines, or in early computers, we were early computers, right? I still call it horsepowering through a problem because I’m a car person.You don’t think that the AI industry has convinced itself that they are AI because that is the machine of our time?I don’t know. I’m not a theory of mind guy. I’m not a cognitive neuroscientist. I think that to believe that what’s going on in your head and my head right now is not a form of computation, you have to be kind of a dualist or you have to be kind of a religious person. You have to think there is some spirit, some soul, some secret sauce of cognition that is not just data entering and being processed and transforming inputs into outputs.Look, I know that is the least romantic, most San Francisco way of explaining what human cognition is. I just have not heard a compelling argument that it is not how our brains work that doesn’t involve some sort of supernatural or immaterial substance.There’s a surprising number of neuroscientists and religious scholars listening to the show. They’re going to come find you.They will.I’m confident. Let me just ask you this. There’s a surprising amount of religiosity in Silicon Valley right now. We just published the Peter Thiel lectures on The Verge. He’s talking about the Antichrist. Do you think these ideas are connected, that we are building God such that they seek God?Yes. I think we will absolutely have AI religions. I think AI is posing all of the same questions as a religion that we would not otherwise be asking of God. “What is our purpose? What is our meaning? Why are we here?” These are the questions that people now talk about in the context of AI.I often tell people that being in San Francisco these days feels like living in Europe during the Reformation, where you just have crazy wild-eyed prophets waving their pamphlets around and trying to get you to join their thing. This is what walking down Market Street in San Francisco feels like.What dropped the scales from your eyes? What made you AGI-pilled?Bing’s Sydney, believe it or not.Yeah?I mean, that was the start. And then from there, it was just kind of a gradual process. One day I realized when I used these things, I wasn’t treating them like an intellectual inferior. I was in some ways treating them as a peer, and that’s when I realized, “Oh, something’s happened here.”So it’s possible I have AI psychosis. It would not be the first time I’ve heard that, but every time that I have thought, “Okay, it can’t possibly get any better than this, this has to be the plateau,” I’ve been wrong.So I’m just learning to approach these things with some humility, and maybe the crazy people who have been predicting that scaling would continue indefinitely are right. If they are, I think we need to learn about them, A, and why they think that, and B, try to figure out what to do about it.Well, Kevin, I’m confident the next time you come on the show, I will have set up a fully AI influencer to make money doing [user-generated content] ads, which is the true future of, I think, all of our businesses.The podcast is Machine Gods. It’s very good. You host it with Casey Newton. And the book is excellent. It’s The AGI Chronicles. Kevin, thank you so much for being on Decoder.Thanks. It was great to see you.Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. content_html_zh:
Today, I’m talking to Kevin Roose, journalist and author of the new book The AGI Chronicles, which details the recent and explosive transformation of the AI industry.

Kevin was a longtime New York Times reporter and host of the popular podcast Hard Fork, but he and friend of the show Casey Newton just left the Times to start the all-new tech podcast Machine Gods, which launched last week.

Kevin and I talked about launching Machine Gods and what it’s like to go from The New York Times to being an independent creator — and then of course we talked about the book, which is an excellently reported dive into the companies racing to build artificial general intelligence.

I wanted to get a sense from Kevin of what it was like to report this, to try and understand these characters and this moment in time, and where it all goes next. Fair warning: This conversation takes a pretty philosophical turn at the end, but I think you’ll find it a really worthwhile back-and-forth.
